title: Kinds of tests and what each one catches
objectives: Define unit, integration, component, contract, end-to-end and smoke tests by what runs for real and what is replaced
Pick the cheapest kind of test that would catch a given bug, and say why the cheaper kinds pass right over it
Explain where each kind runs — Node, a simulated DOM, a real browser, a deployed URL — and what a simulated DOM can't see
Explain how a contract test lets two services check they still agree without deploying both, and why a stubbed client can't

sources.title: web.dev: Three common types of test automation
web.dev: Pyramid or Crab? Find a testing strategy that fits

questions.prompt: A test renders `<CheckoutForm>` with Testing Library in happy-dom, types into the fields, clicks "Pay" and checks the error message. `fetch` is replaced with a double. What kind of test is it?

options.text: A component test — one UI component, driven like a user, in a simulated DOM with the network replaced
An end-to-end test — it clicks buttons and types like a user
A unit test — it only imports one file
A contract test — it checks what the form sends to the API

questions.explanation: Define the kind by what's real: the component and its children are real, the browser is simulated and the network is replaced. Clicking doesn't make it end-to-end — no real browser, backend or database is involved. It renders a whole component tree into a DOM, which is more than a unit test usually means, and nothing here is checked against the real API, so it isn't a contract test.

questions.prompt: `formatDuration(59_999)` prints `"60s"` instead of `"59s"`. What's the cheapest test that catches it?

options.text: A unit test of `formatDuration` with inputs either side of each boundary
An end-to-end test of the page that shows durations
An integration test with the database that stores the durations
A smoke test after deploy

questions.explanation: The bug is entirely inside one pure function, so nothing else needs to be real. A unit test can try `59_999`, `60_000` and `60_001` in microseconds. A browser test could only catch it if some page happened to render exactly that value — slow and unlikely.

questions.prompt: The checkout handler passes the amount in dollars; the payments module expects cents. Both have passing unit tests, and the handler's unit test replaces the payments module with a double. Which test catches the mismatch?

options.text: An integration test that runs the real handler with the real payments module
More unit tests of the payments module
A contract test between the browser and the API
A snapshot of the handler's output

questions.explanation: The bug lives in the wiring between two of your own modules, and the handler's unit test replaced exactly that wiring with a double. Only a test where both are real can see it. More payments-module tests check that module alone, which was never wrong. A contract test is for the boundary between two separately deployed services.

questions.prompt: The orders API renames `total_cents` to `totalCents`. The web app's tests stub the API client with the old shape and stay green; production shows `$NaN`. Which kind of test would have failed **before** the deploy?

options.text: A contract test — the API's CI replays the web app's recorded expectations against the real API
More web-app tests with the same stubbed client
A component test of the order summary
A smoke test against production

questions.explanation: A stub freezes the other team's API at the day you wrote it, so no number of stubbed tests notices a change on their side. Consumer-driven contract testing records what the web app relies on and replays it against the real provider in the provider's pipeline, so the rename fails there. A smoke test would notice — after the deploy, which is too late for "before".

questions.prompt: On a 375px-wide screen, the "Save" button sits under a sticky footer. The component test in happy-dom clicks it and passes. Why?

options.text: happy-dom builds the element tree and fires events but doesn't lay the page out, so nothing is ever "under" anything
happy-dom ignores `z-index` but would catch it with `position: absolute`
The test forgot to set a 375px viewport; with one, happy-dom would fail
`fireEvent.click` uses a different code path than a real click, which is the only difference

questions.explanation: A simulated DOM has no layout engine — `getBoundingClientRect()` returns zeros — so overlap, overflow and positioning bugs are invisible to it whatever the viewport or CSS. An end-to-end test in a real browser catches it: Playwright's click waits for the element to receive events and fails with "intercepts pointer events".

questions.prompt: A deploy ships without the storage provider's environment variable. Every CI check passed. Which test catches it soonest?

options.text: A smoke test run against the deployed URL right after the deploy
An integration test in CI with the storage provider stubbed
A unit test of the upload handler
A contract test against the storage provider's API

questions.explanation: CI runs with its own configuration, so every test there sees a correctly configured app. The bug exists only in the deployed environment, so only a test that runs *against* that environment can see it. A few shallow checks right after deploy turn "users report broken uploads" into a red check a minute later.

questions.prompt: Why do most teams keep end-to-end tests few, compared with unit and integration tests?

options.text: They're slow, need the whole stack running, can fail for reasons unrelated to the change, and point only vaguely at the cause
They find fewer bugs than unit tests
Real browsers can't run in CI
They test the same things as unit tests, so they're redundant

questions.explanation: End-to-end tests give the most confidence per test — they're the only kind that sees the real browser, layout and deployment — but each one costs seconds, a running stack and some flake risk, and a failure still has to be traced to a cause. Headless browsers run fine in CI. They aren't redundant: they catch the layout and wiring bugs the lower levels can't.

prompts.prompt: Name each test by what runs for real.
code: // Real: the pricing module and the cart module, a test Postgres. Replaced: the payment API.
// Real: a browser, the frontend, the API and its database, all running together.
prompts.explanation: Several of your own modules plus a real database, with only the third-party edge replaced, is an integration test. When everything you own is running and a real browser drives it, it's end-to-end. Saying what's real and what's replaced settles the label faster than arguing about it.

prompts.prompt: Fill in the two roles in consumer-driven contract testing.
code: // web app (the ___): its test records "GET /orders/7 → 200 { id, totalCents }" into a pact file
// orders API (the ___): its CI replays the pact against its real handlers
prompts.explanation: The consumer writes the contract from the calls it actually makes; the provider verifies it can still satisfy every recorded interaction. Because the provider runs the check in its own pipeline, a breaking change fails before deploy — without deploying both services together.

prompts.prompt: Tag a sign-in test as a smoke test, then run only the smoke tests against the deployed app.
prompts.explanation: Playwright tags must start with `@`, and `--grep` filters the run by them. The tag name is your choice; the point is a short, fast list of checks that runs against the real deployment, separate from the full suite.

snippets.question: What does this print under Vitest 4 with happy-dom (or jsdom)?
snippets.explanation: Simulated DOMs build the element tree and dispatch events, but they don't lay out the page, so every size and position is zero — an explicit `width:200px` included. That's why component tests in jsdom or happy-dom can't catch overlap, overflow or "button off-screen on mobile" bugs; a real browser can.

code: // Today the real API returns { id: 7, totalCents: 1999 }.
snippets.question: Does the test pass today, and what does production show for order 7?
acceptable: it passes and prod shows NaN
snippets.explanation: The stub still returns last month's shape, so the test is green. In production `order.total_cents` is `undefined`, `undefined / 100` is `NaN`, and `NaN.toFixed(2)` is the string `"NaN"`. A stubbed client checks your code against your memory of the API; a contract test checks it against the API.
